title: Placing an order: an HTTP adapter drives the core, a Postgres adapter plugs into its port, and tests swap in an in-memory adapter
captions: The core holds the business rules. PlaceOrder is a use case. It needs to save orders, so it owns a small interface, OrderRepository. That interface is a port. The core imports no web framework and no SQL driver.
A driving adapter starts the work. The HTTP adapter turns a JSON request into a call to PlaceOrder, and turns the result back into JSON. The core does not know HTTP exists.
A driven adapter is called by the core. The Postgres adapter implements OrderRepository with SQL. Its source code depends on the port, so the arrow points into the core.
In a test, a unit test drives PlaceOrder directly. An in-memory adapter, built on a plain array, implements the same port. The test needs no server and no database, so it runs fast.
Look at the arrows. The adapters know the core. The core knows only its own interfaces. This is the dependency rule: source code dependencies point inward.
